newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia fuel oil price plunges, more losses seen.
newsitem.headline: Asia fuel oil price plunges, more losses seen.

text.p: Asia's high sulphur fuel oil prices have plunged a dramatic 18 percent in the past two weeks, and the price looks set for a further beating, industry sources said on Tuesday.
Ample prompt supplies, high stocks and a sudden drop in demand from key importer China has sent prices tumbling.
Price assessments for benchmark 180-centistoke fuel oil have plunged US$21 per tonne over the past two weeks on the Singapore international market to reach $103 on Tuesday.
Traders in Singapore said February prices were likely to break the psychologically-important $100 per tonne mark soon, which would represent the lowest price in five months.
"We are just putting our hands in the pocket and waiting for prices to bottom," said a trader at a Western oil firm. "I hope, we will not have to wait around for too long."
The underlying derivatives market for fuel oil indicated prices at $98 per tonne Tuesday afternoon.
Fuel oil is mostly used in Asia to generate power and for heavy duty transportation.

The price fall was sparked this month by a sharp fall in imports by China. Normally, China soaks up more than 400,000 tonnes of fuel oil per month, but deliveries in February could be half that amount, traders said.
Last year China demand kept the fuel market tight, but this year extra refining capacity, most noticeably from South Korea, has left excess supplies available.
China built up stocks through December and January for Chinese New Year holidays, which begin on February 7 and were expected to last two weeks.
Traders said more than 100,000 tonnes of fuel oil were overhanging the Singapore market for loading in the next month.
They also cited two to three floating vessels of around 250,000 tonnes each, anchored off southern China, which included unsold fuel oil supplies.
Rumours that some Chinese buyers who bought previously at much higher prices were now reneging on deals have sparked worries even further supplies could find their way on to the market.
The fuel oil plunge has been accompanied by a sharp drop in gas oil and forced refiners to cut production in Singapore in a bid to slow the build-up in stocks and help improve profit margins.
Shell Singapore cut runs at its 435,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) refinery by 30,000 bpd. Esso Singapore reduced output over the weekend at its 230,000-bpd refinery by 20 to 25 percent.
Stocks were also high in Europe and prices soft, which meant Middle East refiners, who operate on much lower costs, were sending their supplies into the Asian market.
With little immediate recovery in the price seen, traders said the market might have to wait until after the Chinese New Year before the slide comes to a halt.
By then, prices could have lost a further $10 per tonne or more, they said.
